chapter_theme: Kuruntokai 381 to 401: the last short akam poems, where one laugh with the shore lord costs a girl her beauty (381) and is then forbidden her (401), the evening and the night become floods to swim (386, 387, 398), pallor parts and closes like well-moss under the lover's touch (399), the friend denies the season to save the man's word (382), and the foster mother reads too late the refused milk of a girl who has gone (396).

381.reading: The friend asks whether the girl, her old beauty gone, her shoulders wasted, her troubled heart sleepless even at night, will turn pale and die: that is all the fruit of once laughing, her bright teeth showing, with the lord of the shore, where white herons cry in the cool fragrant grove and the crosswise waves break, tangling the fresh flowers of the blossoming thicket.
381.nuance: The whole cost is weighed against one laugh (நக்கதன் பயனே): a moment of shown teeth is set against lost beauty, sleeplessness and death. The waves that break and tangle the fresh flowers could be heard as the man who ruined her, but that is a single match of mood, not two pairs, so the shore stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the lament of a girl wasting after the shore lord's absence

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

382.reading: The friend says that the green mullai creeper, made for cool drops, has opened its buds, its scent rising over the bushes with the flower-laden jasmine, because the clouds pour untimely rain: if this were not untimely but the true rainy season, would our lover not have come?
382.nuance: The comfort is an argument from the man's word to the season: since he promised to come with the rains and has not come, these cannot be the rains. The friend turns the proof of his failure into proof that the flowers are mistaken.

thinai_evidence.note: waiting through the season the man named for his return

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the woman, included in நம் காதலோர்

383.reading: The friend tells the girl that because she consented, the friend brought him and the man of the hills has come and stands at the meeting place; now she says today's meeting must wait for another day, and the friend, her hands and feet going slack with distress, trembles like a shoot touched by fire, with nothing she can do.
383.nuance: The friend is caught between the two lovers: she arranged the meeting on the girl's word and must now face the man at the tryst. Line 3 (இன்றை யளவை சென்றைக் கென்றி) is hard to construe; the reading 'not today, another day' is a guess. The colophon's paalai does not fit a tryst on the hill.

thinai_evidence.note: a tryst arranged in kalavu with the man of the hills

comparisons.tenor: the friend trembling in her bind

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the girl, addressed as நீ

384.reading: The friend tells the man that if he enjoys the beauty of the girls, with thick shoulders painted with sugarcane designs, long many-stranded hair and small bangles, and then abandons them, his oath is very fine indeed.
384.nuance: மிகநன்று is praise turned to scorn: the oath he swore is 'very good' precisely because it keeps him free to take and leave. Line 1 (உழுந்துடைக் கழுந்திற்) is unclear: it may name a town of black-gram fields or compare the shoulders to a pounding pestle, so the girls' description is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: the faithless husband of the fields is mocked for his oath

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the man is addressed as மகிழ்ந

385.reading: The girl says the lord of the great mountain slope, where a male monkey of the troop, full of fruit on the jackfruit tree, startled by the hunter's well-aimed bow, leaps like a war-horse so that the tall bamboo of the slope shakes, is always as friendly as on the first day; it is this town with its clamour that is new to her.
385.nuance: She turns the blame from the man to the town: he has not changed, the gossip has. The startled monkey leaping so the bamboo shakes could be read as the lovers disturbed by the town's aim, but only the hunter's aim and the town's talk can be paired, and the poem names no harm, so the monkey stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: jackfruit, monkeys and the hunter's bow of the hill slope

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

386.reading: The woman says that before the lord of the cool shore of spread white sand and crowded flowers left her, she knew evening only as the time that gathers bright-jewelled women for festival; she did not know that evening could be lonely, with a sorrow as wide as the earth.
386.nuance: The same word மாலை closes line 4 and opens line 5, the festival evening turning into the lonely one at the line break. Her ignorance before is part of the complaint: the evening she knew was a public time of women together, the one she learns is private.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore at evening, the hour of neythal

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

387.reading: The woman tells her friend that even if, when the day's limit passes, the mullai blooms and the sun's rays cool their anger, they swim across the helpless evening and reach the night as its bank, what good is it: the flood of night is greater than the sea.
387.nuance: The evening is a river crossed with the night as its far bank; reaching the bank only opens a second water, the night itself, larger than the sea. The poet was named for this line (கங்குல் வெள்ளத்தார்).

thinai_evidence.note: the mullai evening, the hour of waiting

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the friend is addressed as வாழி தோழி

388.reading: The friend tells the man that the row-petalled kuvalai bound to running water does not wither even if summer strikes it, and so the forest, where the dry branches stand like the long line of salt merchants' bullock carts straining at their yokes and the elephant, too weak to split them, folds its trunk and suffers, will be sweet if the girl comes with him.
388.nuance: The lily is never said to be the girl; the friend sets it first and lets the forest follow, and the last line supplies the match. Line 3 (கவணை அன்ன பூட்டுப்பொரு தசாஅ) is hard to construe: the comparison of the yoke is uncertain.

thinai_evidence.note: a proposal that the girl go with the man through the hot forest

comparisons.tenor: the yoke the bulls strain against

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the man is addressed in நும்மொடு

ullurai.tenor: the girl who will go with the man

pairs.situation: she is bound to the man as the lily to running water
the heat of the forest road will not wither her

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a water lily, a thing of the watered land, in a paalai poem, which has no land of its own (porul 1.2), so she does not leave the poem's land (porul 7.27)

389.reading: The friend wishes, friend, that she may get a full meal with ghee-rich quail as its relish: when the man of the great hills came to ask for her in marriage, she said to him 'is it good, son?', and he answered 'it seems good'.
389.nuance: Who is to be feasted, and who said 'is it good, son?', is unclear: என்றனென் is first person, so the friend may be reporting her own question to the suitor, and அத்தை may be a particle rather than a kinswoman. The relish of quail is the reward of good news.

thinai_evidence.note: the man of the hills comes to marry

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the girl is addressed as தோழி

390.reading: Onlookers tell the man, mate of the young she-elephant, not to go on: the day has lost its light, and he should listen to the sound, for a caravan has halted because of the danger of the hostile frontier, and the drum of the guards, who come to the thorn hedge carrying long ringed spears and go back, is sounding.
390.nuance: The onlookers name the man only through the girl, as the tusker of a young cow-elephant, so their warning is for her. The danger is told by sound alone: the caravan has stopped, and the guards' drum carries the frontier's threat after dark.

thinai_evidence.note: onlookers on the road halt a couple journeying together

comparisons.tenor: the girl travelling with the man

thurai_akam.speaker: kandor
thurai_akam.note: the man is addressed as சிறுபிடி துணையே

391.reading: The woman tells her friend that where the bull of the salt ground lay idle without ploughing and the heat had steamed in the rainless scrub, the rain has fallen sweetly, mingled with thunder that strikes so fast the snake's hood shrinks; and in the sorrowful evening that came to leave the separated helpless, the peacock with eyed plumes, sitting on the flowering branch, calls across the wide wet land till it is desolate: they are very foolish.
391.nuance: The peacocks rejoice at the rain that makes her helpless, and she calls them fools for it. The snake whose hood shrinks at the thunder sits beside her own shrinking, but it does nothing a person of the situation does, so it stays scene. Lines 1 and 2 (உவரி யொருத்தல், புகரி புழுங்கிய) are hard to construe.

thinai_evidence.note: the first rains at evening in the scrub

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the friend is addressed as தோழி

392.reading: The friend asks the bright-winged dragonfly, which need fear nothing for carrying good news, to go to the noble one's tall mountain and tell the lord of the hills, where honeycombs hang like the hide shields of kings' marching ranks, that the sister of the weeders who hoe the small millet field crowded with wild cattle is not let out by her kin.
392.nuance: The message is a warning dressed as news: the girl is kept at home by her kin, so the man must come and marry. Calling her the weeders' sister names her as a hill girl of a working family, and the honeycombs like kings' shields make his hill a kingdom fit to send for her.

thinai_evidence.note: millet fields and honeycombs of the hills

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is a dragonfly sent as messenger

393.reading: The friend says the days on which the lover embraced, crushing a garland of mixed flowers, were few; but the gossip is louder than the shout of the Kongar with flashing swords on the day when Athikan, the skilled general of the Pandiyan with green ornaments, fell with his elephant on the battlefield of Vaakai where owls haunt.
393.nuance: The measure of the gossip is a defeat: the Kongar's victory cry over the Pandiyan's fallen general. Whom the husband embraced is not said, so the friend may be scoffing at the scandal of his other women or at the cost of the few days he gave the wife. Athikan, the general, is named in line 4.

thinai_evidence.note: the gossip about the husband's affairs, out of all measure

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

394.reading: The friend says that their laughing play with the man has turned into an enemy, as the soft-headed calf of the big she-elephant with knee-high legs, running and frolicking with the children of the low-eaved huts whom the hill woman of the toddy-rich hamlet bore, was sweet in its early days and later grazed on their millet field.
394.nuance: The calf does no wrong: it grows, and the same play that charmed the children ends in their field being eaten. So the affair has not changed its nature; it has only grown into a thing that costs the girl her standing.

thinai_evidence.note: the elephant calf among the hill people's children and millet

comparisons.tenor: their laughing play with the man

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

395.reading: The woman tells her heart that restraint is beyond her: he, having no love, does not count grace as worth anything and holds firm in his hardness; even if he will not free her as the people here free the moon the snake swallows, there is no one even to say 'fear not' so that her eyes may sleep; pitiable is her shame, if she must leave it to go where he lives.
395.nuance: At an eclipse the people make a din to free the swallowed moon; she is swallowed and no one comes, not even to say a word of comfort. The last two lines are hard: they may mean that shame is pitiable if she leaves home for him, or that it is lost already.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman abandoned by a hard man who has gone away

comparisons.tenor: the rescue he will not give her

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the heart is addressed as நெஞ்சே

396.reading: The foster mother says the girl would not drink her milk or take up her ball, and was weary with her playmates; did she think it easy, then, the going with him through the land where bamboo withers, on the hot slopes of the summer hills, where the tall-tusked bull elephant that gored the dry-branched omai listens for the harsh voice of thundering clouds?
396.nuance: The foster mother reads the signs too late: the refused milk and the dropped ball were the girl's mind already on the road. The elephant listening for thunder that does not come is the drought she now pictures the girl in.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl has left home with her lover

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

397.reading: The friend tells the lord of the shore of strong waters, where the cold wind scatters the millet-like clustered flowers of the full-budded gnaazhal onto the large neythal blossoms as though pouring them, that like a baby who cries 'mother' even while its angry mother beats it, her friend, whether he does her harm or shows her sweet kindness, is within his bounds and has no one else to remove her sorrow.
397.nuance: The baby cries 'mother' to the one who is beating it, because there is no one else to cry to; so the girl's dependence is not a virtue to praise but a helplessness the man is asked to respect. The wind pouring one flower onto another is a gentle image set before the harsh one.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea shore and its flowers

comparisons.tenor: the girl who clings to the man whatever he does

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the man is addressed as சேர்ப்ப

398.reading: The woman tells her friend that they cannot be consoled in the cold time when the spray scatters, in the sorrowful evening when women with carp-like kohl-lined eyes and heavy earrings, cupping their hands as a raft, lift the lamp-flame lit with ghee; those women, when their hard-won lovers come, prepare a feast and, with joy filling their bodies, wipe away the tears that rise.
398.nuance: The lamp-lighting of the evening is seen from outside: other wives shelter the flame and later weep for joy at their men's return. Who the last lines describe is uncertain; they may instead be the friend's promise of a joy the woman refuses to believe in (தேற்றாம்).

thinai_evidence.note: waiting at evening while other women welcome their men

comparisons.tenor: the hands cupped round the lamp

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the friend is addressed as தோழி

399.reading: The woman says her pallor is like the moss at the drinking ghat of the village well: wherever her lover touches, it parts, and wherever he lets go, it spreads again.
399.nuance: The moss parts when a pot or a hand breaks it and closes as soon as the hand is lifted: the pallor is not a slow wasting but a surface that re-forms the moment his touch stops. The doubled தொடுவுழித் தொடுவுழி and விடுவுழி விடுவுழி make the motion repeat in the line.

thinai_evidence.note: the village well with its ghat, a thing of the settled town

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

400.reading: The man tells his charioteer that, resolving with a mind set on good to go the far road and remove without hindrance the love-sickness of the broad-shouldered one, he who is wise and skilled broke across the gravel and led the chariot on a new way through the waste: today he has brought the chariot, and so given grace to her who lived in pain.
400.nuance: The praise goes to the driver, not to the man himself: the charioteer took the shorter, harder way across the gravel because he too thought of the wife. The pain is hers (நோயுழந் துறைவியை), and the gift is the chariot's arrival.

thinai_evidence.note: the return that ends the waiting of the one at home

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer

401.reading: The woman says that even laughing play, one day, with the lord of the shore, where the girls of the orai game, their wet hair crowned with long strands of neythal mixed with choice adumbu flowers, fear the wet crab that scuttles into the sea, has been forbidden: how slight is the friendship of touching bodies!
401.nuance: The play on the beach with flower-crowned girls who shriek at crabs is the most innocent of meetings, and even that is now forbidden: the girl is kept at home. Line 6 (றைதே கம்ம) divides uncertainly; read as ஐதே, 'slight, fragile'.

thinai_evidence.note: shore flowers and crabs of the sea coast

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names no addressee and the colophon gives only the speaker

links.note: In 381 the friend says the girl's wasting and pallor are the only fruit of having laughed with the shore lord; in 401 the girl says that even laughing play with the shore lord has been forbidden.
links.teaches: Read together the two neythal poems show laughter with the shore lord as the whole of kalavu at its smallest unit: one laugh costs the girl her beauty in 381, and in 401 the household guards against exactly that, so the forbidding is the town's answer to the danger the friend names.

links.note: In 66 the friend calls the konrai foolish for taking the untimely rain for the season; in 382 the friend says the rain itself is untimely, since if it were the season the man would have come.
links.teaches: The friend's comfort moves from blaming the tree to denying the season: in 66 nature is fooled by false rain, in 382 the man's promise is made the test of what the rain is, so his word outranks the calendar of flowers.

links.note: Kural 1226: the woman did not know evening brings sickness while her husband had not yet left; in 386 the woman knew evening only as the festival hour of jewelled women and did not know its sorrow wide as the earth.
links.teaches: The poem fills in what the couplet's woman did know of evening before: the public festival hour of the women's gathering, so the Kural's 'I did not know' is the reversal of a known, shared evening into a private sorrow.

links.note: Kural 1167: the woman swims the fierce flood of desire and sees no shore, and at midnight only she is awake; in 387 she swims across the evening to reach the night as its bank, and finds the night's flood larger than the sea.
links.teaches: The couplet's shoreless flood gets its hours in the poem: the evening is the first water and the night a second, larger one, so the shore the Kural's woman cannot see is the bank of evening that only opens onto the night.

links.note: In Akananuru 253 gossip is louder than the cheering at Kudal when the green-jewelled Pandiyan drove out the Kongar; in Kuruntokai 393 gossip is louder than the Kongar's shout when the green-jewelled Pandiyan's general Athikan fell at Vaakai.
links.teaches: The Pandiyan's wars with the Kongar gave akam poets their yardstick for gossip from both outcomes, his victory cheer at Kudal and the enemy's cry over his fallen general, so the measure was the loudest noise of a known war whichever side made it.

links.note: In Akananuru 48 the foster mother asks why the girl will not drink milk and has paled, and the friend tells her of the young hunter; in Kuruntokai 396 the foster mother, after the girl has gone with her man, recalls that she would not drink her milk or take up her ball.
links.teaches: The same symptom, refused milk, stands at two points of one story: in Akananuru 48 it is a question the friend answers in time to open the way to marriage, in Kuruntokai 396 a clue the foster mother reads only after the elopement, so the akam poets used it as the sign that decides whether disclosure or udanpokku follows.

links.note: Kural 1187: she lay in his embrace and turned aside, and at once pallor was on her thick enough to scoop up; in 399 pallor is moss on the village well that parts where he touches and spreads where he lets go.
links.teaches: The couplet's instant hyperbole is given a mechanism by the poem: pallor is a surface like well-moss that closes the moment the hand lifts, so the Kural's 'at that very moment' is not exaggeration but what anyone at a village well has seen.

links.note: Kural 1146: gossip about one day's meeting has spread like the serpent seizing the moon; in 395 the woman says no one frees her as the people here free the moon the snake swallows, nor even tells her not to fear.
links.teaches: The eclipse served both as a spectacle everyone sees and as a rite in which everyone rushes to help: the Kural takes the first sense for gossip, the poem the second for rescue, and the woman's complaint is that her eclipse draws the town's eyes but none of its help.

links.note: In Akananuru 34 the man, his work done, bids the charioteer drive fast so that his wife may regain her beauty; in Kuruntokai 400 the man thanks the charioteer who cut a new way across the gravel and brought the chariot home to the wife in pain.
links.teaches: The two poems are the command and the thanks of one homeward drive: Akananuru 34 asks for speed, Kuruntokai 400 credits the charioteer with the resolve and the shortcut, so the driver is shown sharing the husband's care for the wife and earns praise for it.

links.note: In 7 onlookers on the road ask who the pitiable bowman and his anklet-wearing girl are, setting out into the wilds; in 390 onlookers tell the man, mate of the young she-elephant, to stop for the night because of the frontier guards' drum.
links.teaches: The onlookers of udanpokku move from pity to protection: in 7 they only wonder at the couple, in 390 they name the danger of the road at nightfall and halt them, so the kandor are not only witnesses of the elopement but its guardians on the way.

source_issues: kuruntokai:382 line 3, 392 line 8 and 394 line 4 are repaired readings (flags); marked as printed.
kuruntokai:396: the colophon thinai is printed பாால; read as பாலை.
kuruntokai:383: the colophon's paalai does not fit a tryst with the man of the hills at the meeting place; inferred kurinji.
kuruntokai:398: colophon paalai; the poem is a woman waiting at evening, inferred mullai.
kuruntokai:381 and 395 have no poet in the colophon.

kuruntokai:381-401: the colophons give only the speaker (… கூற்று), so thurai_akam addressees are taken from vocatives in the poems where present and given as pira otherwise, and occasion.words is null.
Hard lines: 383 line 3, 384 line 1, 388 line 3, 389 lines 1-2, 391 lines 1-2, 395 lines 7-8, 398 lines 6-8, 401 line 6; readings marked uncertain.
